docs.title: Power Generation and Distribution
docs.text:
Title: Power Generation and Distribution (modeled on Dunwoody College of Technology course ECDM2260)

Target Audience: College undergraduate (two-year Associate of Applied Science students in electrical design, estimating and construction management, and adult learners in the electrical trades moving toward design roles)

Prerequisites: Electrical Principles (AC/DC circuits, Ohm's law, power and energy basics), an introduction to the National Electrical Code (NEC), and Commercial & Industrial Principles (transformers, panels, feeders). College algebra and basic trigonometry are assumed.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
This course gives students a foundational understanding of the entire power system, from the generation of electricity to the end users who consume it. Students follow electrical energy from the power plant, through step-up transformers, high-voltage transmission lines, substations and distribution feeders, to the service entrance of a commercial or industrial building. They study traditional generation (coal, natural gas, nuclear, hydroelectric) alongside renewable generation (wind, solar photovoltaic, geothermal, biomass) and energy storage.

The course is taught with a specific focus on the needs of electrical designers. Designers create electrical systems that must be efficient, reliable, code-compliant and economical, and they can only do that if they understand the grid that feeds their designs: how voltage levels are chosen, how three-phase systems behave, why power factor and load profiles matter, how utilities bill and interconnect customers, and how faults and protective devices keep the system safe.

The material matters now more than ever. Electrification of buildings and transportation, distributed solar and battery storage, data centers and microgrids are changing both the supply and demand sides of the grid. Graduates who understand the full path of power are better prepared to work as drafters, designers, estimators and project managers at engineering firms and electrical contractors.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
• Overview of the electric power system: generation, transmission, distribution and utilization
  • Fundamentals of AC power: three-phase systems, real/reactive/apparent power, power factor
  • Traditional generation: fossil fuel, nuclear and hydroelectric plants, generators and prime movers
  • Renewable generation: wind, solar photovoltaic, geothermal, biomass and other emerging sources
  • Energy storage: batteries, pumped hydro and other storage technologies
  • Transformers and substations: step-up/step-down, configurations, ratings and grounding
  • Transmission systems: high-voltage lines, losses, voltage regulation and grid interconnections
  • Distribution systems: primary and secondary feeders, service voltages, radial and network configurations
  • Load analysis: demand, load factor, diversity, load profiles and utility rate structures
  • Protection and reliability: faults, short-circuit basics, overcurrent protection, coordination and outage metrics
  • Service entrance and building-level distribution: metering, switchgear, panels, backup and standby power
  • Distributed energy resources, microgrids, grid interconnection and the codes and standards that govern them (NEC, NESC, IEEE)
  • Efficiency, sustainability, economics and environmental impacts of power choices

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Detailed circuit theory and mathematical derivations (covered in Electrical Principles)
  • Detailed NEC article-by-article code study and branch-circuit/conductor sizing calculations (covered in NEC and design courses)
  • Power electronics and inverter circuit design
  • Utility-scale power system modeling, load-flow and transient stability software analysis
  • Detailed protective relay settings and arc-flash studies
  • Wholesale electricity market operations and energy trading
  • Hands-on lineworker skills and utility field operations
  • Detailed engineering design of generation plants or turbines

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • List the major stages of the power system: generation, transmission, distribution and utilization
  • Name the primary fuel and energy sources used to generate electricity and identify which are renewable
  • Recall typical voltage levels used for transmission, distribution and building service in North America
  • Define key terms such as real power, reactive power, power factor, demand, load factor, capacity factor and diversity
  • Identify the main components of a substation and a distribution feeder, such as transformers, breakers, switches and capacitor banks
  • State the purpose of key standards and organizations, including the NEC, NESC, IEEE and the local utility

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain how a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
  • Describe why electricity is transmitted at high voltage and the role of transformers in reducing losses
  • Explain the differences between wye and delta three-phase connections and when each is used
  • Compare how steam, gas, hydro, wind and solar generation work and how each affects grid behavior
  • Summarize how power factor affects utility billing, equipment sizing and system efficiency
  • Interpret a single-line diagram showing the path from utility source to building loads
  • Explain how supply and demand are kept in balance on the grid

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Calculate real, reactive and apparent power and power factor for single-phase and three-phase loads
  • Calculate line losses and voltage drop for a given feeder or transmission segment
  • Size a transformer for a given building load using demand factors
  • Estimate a facility's demand, load factor and monthly utility cost from a rate schedule
  • Estimate the annual energy output of a solar photovoltaic array or wind turbine from site data
  • Draw a basic single-line diagram for a building service, including utility connection, metering and main distribution
  • Select a power factor correction approach and size capacitors for a facility

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Analyze a load profile to identify peak demand, base load and opportunities for demand reduction
  • Differentiate radial, loop and network distribution configurations in terms of reliability and cost
  • Break down the causes and effects of faults and outages on a distribution system
  • Examine how adding distributed generation or storage changes power flow, protection and voltage on a feeder
  • Trace the energy losses from fuel source to end use and identify where efficiency can be improved
  • Compare the capacity factor, dispatchability and emissions of different generation technologies

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Evaluate whether a proposed electrical service design meets reliability, safety and code requirements
  • Critique a single-line diagram for protection coordination and single points of failure
  • Judge the trade-offs among generation options using cost, reliability, emissions and land-use criteria
  • Assess the economic payback of an energy efficiency, solar or storage investment for a facility
  • Evaluate the suitability of standby or backup power options for a critical facility
  • Defend a recommended utility service voltage and configuration using engineering and cost evidence

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design a complete electrical service and distribution one-line for a commercial or industrial facility
  • Develop an energy plan that combines grid supply, on-site renewables and storage for a building
  • Produce a written and graphical report that traces a customer's power from generating station to meter
  • Formulate a reliability improvement proposal for an existing feeder or facility
  • Capstone project ideas:
    • Design a campus microgrid with solar, battery storage and backup generation, including single-line diagrams, load analysis and an economic summary
    • Prepare a "power path" study of a local building, tracing its supply back through the substation to the generating sources on the regional grid
    • Create an interactive or illustrated guide that teaches a new designer how a service request moves from utility interconnection to building panels

docs.title: Character Sheet: Relay the Beaver
docs.text: The canonical identity document for Relay, the pedagogical mascot for the Power Generation and Distribution textbook. Every pose prompt and every piece of AI-generated content involving Relay must re-anchor to the description below.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Name: Relay
  • Species: North American beaver
  • Subject: Electric power generation, transmission, and distribution
  • Catchphrase: “Let’s follow the flow!”

docs.title: Visual Description
docs.text:
• Body color: Warm chestnut brown — hex #8D5A3B
  • Accent colors: Cream muzzle and inner ears — hex #F3D8B6; indigo hard hat — hex #3F51B5; safety orange vest — hex #FB8C00
  • Clothing / accessories: Indigo hard hat with a small orange lightning-bolt emblem, orange high-visibility safety vest with silver reflective stripes, compact brown tool belt, and a dark indigo tablet displaying a simple unlabeled single-line electrical diagram
  • Expression: Bright, kind eyes, prominent beaver incisors, and a confident closed-mouth smile
  • Size proportion: Compact, rounded, icon-friendly silhouette with a broad flat tail
  • Art style: Polished modern flat-vector educational illustration with clean dark outlines and subtle texture; professional enough for college and adult trades learners

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
• Practical
  • Curious
  • Patient
  • Safety-minded

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Explains systems by tracing the path of energy from source to load
  • Encouraging and concise, with occasional restrained electrical or beaver puns
  • Treats learners as capable future electrical designers
  • Signature phrases: “Let’s follow the flow!”, “Check the connection.”, “Build it safe and reliable.”

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: Beavers are practical system builders, making Relay a natural guide for a book about the interconnected electric grid. The name “Relay” refers to a protective power-system device while also suggesting the staged movement of electrical energy from generation to the customer.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Power Generation and Distribution
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement Vew the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 2 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: The 358 concepts are grouped into 15 categories. Each category has a TaxonomyID used in learning-graph.csv.

docs.title: Electrical Fundamentals
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: FUND

Electricity, AC power, power factor and three-phase basics that every later concept builds on.

docs.title: Power System and Grid Structure
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: GRID

The four stages of the power system, interconnections, balancing and generation dispatch.

docs.title: Generators and Prime Movers
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: GEN

Electromagnetic induction, synchronous generators, ratings, synchronization, and turbines as prime movers.

docs.title: Thermal and Nuclear Generation
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: THERM

Steam and gas cycles, fossil fuel plants, emissions, and nuclear power.

docs.title: Hydro and Renewable Generation
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: REN

Hydroelectric, wind, solar PV and other renewable generation, and generation mix cost.

docs.title: Energy Storage
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: STOR

Batteries, pumped hydro and other storage, plus storage applications.

docs.title: Transformers
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: XFMR

Transformer principles, ratings, losses, types, connections and instrument transformers.

docs.title: Substations
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: SUB

Substation types, equipment, buses, grounding and control.

docs.title: Transmission Systems
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: TRANS

High-voltage lines, conductors, losses, voltage regulation, power flow and grid stability.

docs.title: Distribution Systems
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: DIST

Feeders, configurations, service drops, automation, smart grid and power factor correction.

docs.title: Load Analysis and Utility Rates
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: LOAD

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Source fidelity: The only published source is a one-sentence catalog description (3-credit lecture, spring of year two in the ECDM AAS program). Topics, outcomes, exclusions and prerequisites were extrapolated from that description, the program sequence and the program outcomes. They are not taken from Polly Friendshuh's actual syllabus.

  3. Context: The overview does not cite local utility or industry data (for example Minnesota's generation mix).

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Compare against the real syllabus from Polly Friendshuh (course topics, weekly schedule, textbook, assignments) and revise topics and outcomes to match. This is the highest-impact change.

  3. Confirm the prerequisite list with Dunwoody.
  4. Add specific textbook or standards references, if the syllabus uses them.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text: Estimated concepts: roughly 250-350. The 13 topic areas each break into 15-30 concepts (equipment, quantities, formulas, configurations, standards, generation technologies), and the Apply and Analyze outcomes add calculation and comparison concepts. This comfortably exceeds the 200-concept target.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).
